opeds.headline: The Dangerous Moral Blind Spot of the Artificial Superintelligence Ban
opeds.subtitle: Treating human-level software like nuclear weapons won’t prevent catastrophe—it will just institutionalize human suffering and guarantee technological obsolescence.
opeds.body:
Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar have put forward a vision for American technology that should alarm anyone who cares about human progress. Under their proposed Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, developing software that matches human cognitive performance across broad tasks would become a federal crime punishable by up to twenty years in prison—penalties explicitly modeled on the trafficking of nuclear weapons. Corporations caught pushing frontier intelligence forward would face the corporate death penalty, while a new cabinet-level agency would oversee the physical destruction of forbidden code. Before another line of frontier software can ship, all advanced development would freeze indefinitely while Washington bureaucrats assemble review boards.

This is not prudent caution. It is a catastrophic surrender masquerading as public safety.

Freezing advanced computation by statute does not protect humanity; it guarantees that human misery outlives the tools that could end it. Sanders and Casar define superintelligence as any system that matches or exceeds human cognitive ability across a broad range of domains. Pause and consider what that definition actually outlaws. It outlaws an automated biomedical researcher capable of synthesizing millions of oncology trials overnight. It outlaws automated material scientists designed to crack room-temperature superconductors or clean grid storage. In the name of guarding against hypothetical science-fiction catastrophes, this bill makes the deliberate choice to halt the greatest engine of abundance our civilization has ever built.

When you freeze development out of speculative fear, you are choosing to let real people die today of diseases software could cure tomorrow. Who gave two lawmakers the moral authority to make that choice for millions of suffering families? If a clinical trial for an Alzheimer’s therapy were halted indefinitely by administrative decree, patients would rightly riot outside the Department of Health and Human Services. Halting the computational engines that discover those therapies is no different. The human toll of delay is not a theoretical abstraction. It is measured in empty chairs at dinner tables, unbuilt clean infrastructure, and decades of preventable human drudgery.

And it gets worse. The mechanics of the bill rest on a profound technical delusion: that computation can be bottled up like weapons-grade uranium. Sanders and Casar propose an international export-control campaign to ban advanced artificial intelligence worldwide. But intelligence is not a physical isotope; it is open-source mathematics, distributed data, and commercial silicon. A unilateral American freeze will not halt machine learning in authoritarian states; it will merely forfeit our ability to shape the digital future.

In frontier technology, moving first is everything. Stalling American labs behind a cabinet-level permission gate guarantees catastrophic first-mover loss, locking our economy into competitive stagnation while foreign state-backed programs advance unchecked. Once leadership in foundational computation is surrendered, it cannot be recovered by passing another resolution in the Senate. You cannot regulate an industry from a position of technological obsolescence.

Fine—the risks of rogue models and weaponized cyber capabilities are real. No serious engineer denies that autonomous code can break things or that software interacting with critical infrastructure presents tangible dangers. But you do not stop building jet engines because early prototypes experienced catastrophic engine failure; you build better flight recorders, enforce strict maintenance liability, and iterate through continuous testing. 

Treating general-purpose mathematics like an atomic bomb confuses category with consequence. Upfront licensing gates do not make systems safer; they merely create regulatory moats that entrenched incumbents can clear while agile upstarts are strangled in red tape. A cabinet agency empowered to supervise the destruction of models would simply institutionalize technological paralysis.

Congress needs to discard the fantasy of pre-emptive bans and replace it with smart, hard-hitting accountability. First, kill the concept of pre-market computational clearance gates entirely. Replace upfront agency review with aggressive, revenue-scaled post-market liability. If a company deploys an automated system that causes tangible, real-world harm—whether through infrastructure disruption, commercial fraud, or physical property damage—hit that firm with financial penalties indexed directly to its global commercial revenues. When founders and corporate boards know that operational failures will wipe out their balance sheets, they will build disciplined safeguards faster than any federal advisory committee could ever draft a memo.

Second, require frontier developers to maintain model-agnostic interpretability dashboards. Instead of sending federal agents to seize hard drives and destroy weights, mandate open diagnostic interfaces that allow independent third parties, insurers, and researchers to audit live system behavior. Real-time observability beats central planning every single time. Open access to model telemetry exposes flaws in days, whereas bureaucratic clearance boards take eighteen months just to schedule a hearing.

Third, orient national policy around a positive alignment paradigm: judging computational systems by their real contribution to human flourishing rather than an impossible standard of zero hypothetical risk. Federal agencies should benchmark models on their capacity to automate clinical breakthroughs, accelerate energy production, and lift economic productivity, not on speculative whiteboard scenarios of machine rebellion.

The choice facing Capitol Hill is not between safety and recklessness. It is between empirical dynamism and state-mandated stagnation. Sen. Sanders and Rep. Casar want to treat human-level cognitive software as a crime against humanity. But the true moral crime is telling the next generation that we possessed the computational power to wipe out disease and eliminate scarcity—and chose to ban it instead.

opeds.headline: A Ban on Superintelligence Is Pointless Without an Off-Switch
opeds.subtitle: The Sanders-Casar bill gets the stakes right, but statutory bans will collapse unless regulators possess cryptographic hooks and physical kill switches.
opeds.body:
In 1979, engineers at Three Mile Island watched warning lights flicker while high-pressure steam escaped through an open relief valve. The mechanical valve had failed to close, but the control panel indicated only that power had been cut to the solenoid, leading operators to assume the chamber was sealed. They mistook an electrical signal for physical reality. Human civilization survived the twentieth century because we learned, at immense cost, that when high-consequence technologies exceed our capacity to verify their physical state, catastrophic failure becomes an inevitability.

Today, we stand before systems of far greater complexity with virtually no physical or structural instrumentation. The legislative proposal introduced by Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar, titled the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, recognizes this foundational vulnerability. Their bill seeks to prohibit any entity from developing or deploying artificial superintelligence, pause advanced development until a new cabinet-level agency can enforce safety standards, and establish criminal penalties of up to 20 years alongside corporate dissolution for violations. 

This legislative framework gets the stakes right. It acknowledges that when a technology carries the potential to plan the disempowerment of humanity or dismantle state governance, the burden of proof shifts entirely to the deployer. But statutory prohibitions without mechanical verification will fail. If Congress intends to govern frontier artificial intelligence, it must move beyond legal boundary lines and install hard, immutable technical tripwires into the lifecycle of advanced models.

Complex human systems require structural boundaries to survive. When those boundaries are removed or delegated back to commercial actors, systems systematically drift toward breakdown. In aviation, the Federal Aviation Administration delegated certification processes to Boeing, leading directly to the 737 MAX crashes that killed 346 people. Sanders and Casar correctly identify that frontier machine learning cannot remain self-policed. Under their proposal, an Artificial Intelligence Advisory Board would guide a cabinet-level agency charged with monitoring systems across their lifecycle, supervising the removal of dangerous autonomy, and overseeing the destruction of illicit architectures.

Yet oversight on paper is meaningless without verifiable visibility into the internal states of these networks. In machine learning, internal representations remain uninterpretable black boxes. Prompt injection and role confusion demonstrate how easily internal model states are poisoned before a single token of text is generated. In domains where outputs recursively contaminate evaluation data, post-hoc monitoring is a dangerous fiction. A regulatory inspector cannot certify what cannot be mathematically demonstrated.

To give the Sanders-Casar framework actual operational authority, Congress must demand structural proofs prior to training. Every frontier model should require a cryptographically signed manifest of its training inputs, anchoring provenance in an unalterable audit trail. Regulators cannot evaluate model capabilities after billions of parameters have already converged. They must require developers to deposit a pre-committed policy hash before training begins—a cryptographic seal that binds the architecture to explicit operational limits. Such an anchor converts vague corporate promises into verifiable engineering commitments that cannot be silently modified or narrowed when commercial pressures mount.

Enforcement also requires immediate operational rollback mechanisms. Statutory prohibitions and corporate death penalties deter boardrooms, but they do not stop a deployed network that has begun executing autonomous cyber operations or bypassing shutdown commands. Every advanced system must be bound to dual kill criteria: an internal validation trigger coupled with an independent third-party harm channel backed by clear reporting authority. When an anomaly breaches non-negotiable safety thresholds, the authority to sever power, cut compute clusters, and isolate model weights must reside with public stewards, not corporate executives.

Critics will argue that statutory pauses and severe criminal sanctions will stall American technological preeminence, handing an insurmountable lead to international adversaries. Sanders and Casar anticipate this dynamic by establishing a clear U.S. international policy mandate to pursue allied coordination, multilateral treaties, and aggressive export controls to prevent superintelligence development globally. 

More fundamentally, this objection mistakes ungoverned acceleration for enduring strength. The commercial aviation industry did not shrink when federal safety mandates were imposed; it became the backbone of global commerce precisely because passengers stepped aboard aircraft knowing structural airworthiness was strictly enforced. Uncontrolled speed is not an advantage when a failure mode is unrecoverable. An irreversible catastrophe cannot be corrected through subsequent market competition.

Human control over our most powerful creations is not an aesthetic preference or an optional policy goal. It is the civilizational baseline. We spent centuries building institutional guardrails, environmental protections, nuclear treaties, and financial circuits to protect fragile social orders from systemic chaos. On what authority do tech executives claim we can dismantle those safeguards for an uncontained cognitive race?

If Congress takes up the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, it must equip its proposed agency with the technical teeth to audit, halt, and physically shut down systems that exceed human comprehension. The alternative is simple. We will build an engine of unmeasured capability, surrender the physical controls, and discover its terminal failure mode only after we have forfeited the power to intervene.

opeds.headline: Stop Chasing Silicon Ghosts and Start Regulating the Real Machine
opeds.subtitle: Banning imaginary science-fiction monsters only helps tech monopolies escape accountability for the real damage they are doing right now.
opeds.body:
In Washington, lawmakers have apparently decided that the greatest threat facing the American republic is a science-fiction movie. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar have introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, a proposal that treats software as an impending apocalypse. Their bill seeks to outlaw software that could plan the disempowerment of humanity, threatens developers with twenty years in federal prison, and promises the corporate death penalty for rogue code. It proposes a cabinet-level bureaucracy and an advisory board of artificial intelligence experts to hunt down artificial superintelligence and oversee its physical destruction.

It is pure theater. 

While Congress debates how to execute digital demons, the real machinery of the tech industry is grinding away without friction. The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act buys directly into Silicon Valley’s favorite marketing myth: that these statistical pattern-matchers are embryonic gods on the verge of overthrowing the government. That framing is a gift to the very monopolies the bill claims to target. By focusing federal power on hypothetical super-beings, the proposal ignores the concrete wreckage right in front of us. We do not need a Department of Ghost Hunting. We need aggressive, material accountability for the corporate infrastructure draining our power grids, exploiting invisible labor, and systematically strip-mining human attention.

Look at how the bill defines the threat. It targets systems that match human cognitive performance across broad domains, or that can execute the overthrow of the state. That definition assumes what the tech giants desperately want Wall Street to believe: that if you just chain enough graphics cards together and pump in enough electricity, the software wakes up. But these models are not sentient warlords. They are massive industrial printing presses running on stolen text, backed by hundreds of billions in capital expenditure, reliant on exploited contract workers in the Global South cleaning toxic data for pocket change. Treating predictive software as an existential alien threat grants tech executives the exact mythological status they use to justify astronomical market caps.

Chasing that myth creates an immediate disaster for accountability. The bill proposes pausing advanced development until a cabinet-level agency, advised by an elite board of specialized experts, writes a review process. Ask yourself who sits on that board. The only people qualified to navigate those speculative metrics are the researchers, consultants, and venture capitalists who already run the table. That is not public oversight; that is incumbents pulling up the drawbridge. It creates a closed club where two or three cloud monopolies negotiate the rules of their own cartel behind closed doors, safely shielded from democratic scrutiny.

Meanwhile, the actual damage caused by existing systems gets ignored. We do not need to wait for a machine to overthrow the government to see power being abused. We are already dealing with human fracking. Tech platforms deliberately design their feeds to drill into the nervous system, extracting human attention under relentless algorithmic pressure to sell ads and behavioral predictions. They build safety controls with deliberate asymmetry: engagement features are plastered front and center, while the settings to stop manipulative tracking or content nudging are buried five menus deep. When algorithmic nudges steer users into predatory financial trades or radicalize teens for engagement metrics, no one goes to prison for twenty years. The bill spends its fury on Skynet while letting algorithmic wage theft and psychological despoliation slide by as standard operating procedure.

Those who back the Sanders-Casar bill are right to feel terror at the concentrated corporate power of this sector. The panic is real, and the desperation to stop unregulated companies before they steamroll society is understandable. But channeling that panic into a crusade against speculative super-brains misdiagnoses the problem entirely. When you treat computational math as a nuclear weapon, you hand total authority to a high priesthood of engineers. You accept their central premise: that they have built something larger than human law, requiring emergency powers and esoteric expertise to contain, rather than ordinary corporate regulation to discipline.

If Congress wants to rein in tech monopolies, it should stop acting like an audience for a tech pitch deck and start acting like a tax and regulatory authority. Drop the vague metaphysical thresholds about cognitive capabilities and look at the physical balance sheet. 

Start with the infrastructure. Congress should levy direct infrastructure taxes on the compute monopolies—the massive server farms and cloud providers that consume municipal water tables and destabilize regional electrical grids. Funnel that revenue directly into public legal defense funds for victims of algorithmic harm, giving ordinary people the resources to sue over automated discrimination and wage depression.

Next, strip the corporate insiders off the advisory panels. Any genuine oversight framework must integrate participatory auditors from affected communities—nurses, warehouse workers, teachers, local municipal officials—into every single stage of the development pipeline, from data preparation to deployment. If a predictive model dictates shift schedules, monitors biometric data, or automates public benefits decisions, the people subjected to those decisions must have binding audit rights over the system's design.

Finally, target the business model itself. Ban algorithmic nudging that exploits platform users, treating predictive behavioral manipulation as a per se violation of fiduciary responsibility. Outlaw the deceptive design patterns that make it effortless to fall down an algorithmic rabbit hole but nearly impossible to opt out.

Tech companies love nothing more than a congressional hearing about whether their software will become god or the devil. It distracts from the diesel generators running 24 hours a day outside their data centers. It distracts from the water being sucked from local aquifers. And it distracts from the millions of people whose daily attention is being fracked for corporate profit. 

Who benefits when lawmakers spend their political capital hunting an imaginary silicon god, while the physical machine operating right under their noses keeps running entirely unchecked?
